Here are my verse-by-verse notes from the sources I could access. Due to search limits, I couldn't reach all denominational pages; where a tradition's distinctive reading is missing, I note that clearly.

---

## Galatians 1 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: *"Paul, an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead—"*

**Traditional reading (Evangelical / Reformed):**

Paul immediately defends his apostolic authority because the Judaizers in Galatia were undermining it. "Apostle" means "sent one" — one commissioned with official representative status. Paul insists his calling neither originated *from* men nor came *through* the agency of any man; it was direct and divine, from both Jesus Christ and God the Father. The mention of the resurrection is pointed: Paul's call came from the risen, glorified Christ, not from Jesus in His earthly ministry (as with the Twelve). This makes his apostleship in one sense even more illustrious. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/ ; Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

Martin Luther (cited by both Enduring Word and Precept Austin) said: "When I was a young man I thought Paul was making too much of his call… We exalt our calling, not to gain glory among men… but because people need to be assured that the words we speak are the words of God." *(Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-1-commentary)*

Charles Spurgeon: Paul's enemies said "Paul was never one of the Saviour's twelve apostles… No doubt he has borrowed his doctrine from them." Paul's retort: "I am an apostle as truly as any other of the twelve; 'not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ.'" *(Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-1-commentary)*

Ellicott notes that Paul's blunt double denial ("not of men, neither by man") uses two different Greek prepositions — *apo* (source/origin) and *dia* (intermediate agency) — to shut down any claim that his commission was human in either origin or channel. *(Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/1.htm)*

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik (Enduring Word) represents a broadly charismatic-evangelical reading. He emphasizes that Paul's apostleship "was not based on opinion polls and it did not come from any human council." The direct, supernatural nature of the call is highlighted. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

**Lutheran:** Not retrieved due to search limits.

---

### v. 2: *"and all the brothers with me, To the churches of Galatia:"*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul includes "all the brothers with me" — his co-workers — not because they co-authored the letter (note the "I" in v. 6), but to show that his message had the united support of those around him. The letter is addressed to multiple congregations ("churches," plural) across the region of Galatia, not a single city-church — underscoring how widespread the problem was. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill notes the plural "churches" shows the New Testament pattern was congregational, not national or provincial. Though disorderly and swerving from the faith, they are still called "churches" — but notably without warm epithets Paul uses for other churches (e.g., "beloved of God," "called to be saints"), hinting at his dismay. *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

Ellicott discusses at length whether "Galatia" refers to the ethnic northern region or the wider Roman province (including southern cities like Lystra and Derbe). He concludes the narrower, ethnic sense is more likely. *(Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/1.htm)*

---

### v. 3: *"Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,"*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul's standard greeting merges the Greek *charis* (grace) and the Hebrew *shalom* (peace). Martin Luther called these two words the sum of Christianity: "These two terms, grace and peace, constitute Christianity." Paul always puts grace before peace — grace is the root, peace the fruit. The double source ("from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ") quietly affirms Christ's equality with the Father. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/ ; Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-1-commentary)*

Spurgeon: "Peace before grace would be perilous; nay more, it would be ruinous." *(Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-1-commentary)*

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik notes that Paul used "grace" over 100 times in his writings, while all other NT writers combined use it only 55 times — Paul was "truly the apostle of grace." *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

---

### v. 4: *"who gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,"*

**Traditional reading (substitutionary atonement):**

This verse gives the gospel in a nutshell. Jesus "gave Himself" — a voluntary, self-determined sacrifice. It was "for our sins" — substitutionary and expiatory, not merely exemplary. The purpose is rescue ("deliver us") from "this present evil age" — not removal from the world's presence but deliverance from its dominating power. All of this is "according to the will of our God and Father" — the cross was God's plan, not plan B. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Spurgeon stressed the substitutionary character: "Christ never gave himself for our righteousness; but he gave himself for our sins… The heart of the gospel is redemption, and the essence of redemption is the substitutionary sacrifice of Christ." And: "Christ died for our sins, not for our virtues. It is not your efficiencies, but your deficiencies which entitle you to the Lord Jesus." *(Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-1-commentary)*

John Calvin (cited by Enduring Word): "These words… are very important. He wanted to tell the Galatians straight out that atonement for sins and perfect righteousness are not to be sought anywhere but in Christ." *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill carefully distinguishes: Christ gave not just "his own things" but "himself" — body, soul, entire human nature in union with His divine person. The deliverance is from the damning power and governing influence of all that is evil in this world — Satan's dominion, sinful lusts, vain living, and eternal destruction. All was "according to the will of God" — by divine decree and purpose, not human deserving. *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics section): "The foundation of the gospel is self-sacrifice… If our sins had been removed at some meaner cost than the blood of the Son of God, we should be disposed to say that sin is after all a light thing in God's sight." *(BibleHub Homiletics — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/galatians/1.htm)*

**Reformed (Desiring God / John Piper):** Piper links v. 4 to v. 1: just as Paul's apostleship is "not from men," so the gospel itself is not from men. The cross is God's work, not man's. Piper emphasizes that the gospel of grace is under attack by those adding law-works, and v. 4 is Paul's compressed summary of the true gospel he defends. *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/this-is-not-mans-gospel)*

---

### v. 5: *"to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen."*

**Traditional reading:**

This doxology likely ascribes glory to both the Father and the Son. False teaching robbed God of glory; Paul's opening doxology re-centres everything on God's glory as the ultimate purpose of salvation. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill says the doxology is directed either to Christ (for giving Himself), to the Father (for willing it), or to both — showing the greatness of the blessing and the grateful response it deserves. *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

---

### v. 6: *"I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—"*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul omits his usual thanksgiving for the recipients — the only letter where he does so (Lightfoot). He is "amazed" (Greek *thaumazō*) — not merely at their turning, but at how *quickly* they are doing it. Notably, they are deserting not merely a doctrine but a Person — "the One who called you." To abandon the true gospel is to abandon God Himself. The phrase "by the grace of Christ" underscores that their calling was entirely of grace, which makes their turn to law-keeping all the more tragic. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Ellicott debates the meaning of "so soon": it may refer to the short time since their conversion (c. AD 51), or the short time since Paul's last visit. He leans toward the latter but notes that "soon" is relative. *(Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/1.htm)*

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** Piper says it is "astonishing when a person hears and believes the gospel but afterward turns away from it." The underlying truth of the whole passage (vv. 6–10) is that "there is only one gospel." *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-not-to-believe-an-angel)*

---

### v. 7: *"which is not even a gospel. Evidently some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ."*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul makes a wordplay using two Greek words for "another": *heteros* (different in kind) and *allos* (another of the same kind). The false teachers probably claimed their message was simply an alternative gospel of the same sort. Paul retorts: it is *different in kind* — so different that it is "not even a gospel" (not good news at all). Three things are said about it: (1) it is illegitimate — "not another" of the same kind; (2) it brings trouble, not peace; (3) it is a perversion/distortion of the true gospel of Christ. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Luther (cited by Enduring Word): "Note the resourcefulness of the devil. Heretics do not advertise their errors… the devil masquerades… He puts on white to make himself look like an angel of light." *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill: Paul "corrects himself for calling their false doctrine by the name of another Gospel" — it does not deserve the name "gospel" at all. *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

**Reformed (Piper):** Paul "did not mean to say that there are several possible gospels… there is no other gospel than the one he preached to them." Universalism (all roads lead to heaven) is "a radical and forthright denial" made by this text. *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-not-to-believe-an-angel)*

---

### vv. 8–9: *"But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse! As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse!"*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul pronounces a double *anathema* (curse, devoted to destruction) on anyone — himself included hypothetically, or even an angel — who preaches a different gospel. The curse is not merely on the message but on the messenger. The double pronouncement (v. 8 and v. 9) intensifies the solemnity. Paul's "love" here is for souls in danger of hell: a false gospel is "a rescue ship about to sink." The language echoes the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 27. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

**Reformed (Piper):** "When a person is anathema, he is cut off from Christ (Romans 9:3) and doomed to eternal punishment." The text is a warning that "rejection of that gospel leaves a person under God's curse." Piper uses this to argue against pluralism: there are not many roads to heaven. *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-not-to-believe-an-angel)*

---

### v. 10: *"Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ."*

**Traditional reading:**

Having just pronounced a curse, Paul anticipates the charge that he is trying to win friends. He insists his first audience is God, not men. "Servant" is better translated "bondservant" or "slave" (*doulos*) — not a voluntary, part-time helper but one wholly owned by his Master. Paul contrasts himself with the false teachers, who apparently shaped their message to please their audience. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

**Reformed (Piper):** "Two things are at stake when the gospel is perverted: one is the glory of Christ; the other is the salvation of sinners. If the gospel is twisted, the all-sufficiency of Christ's work is dishonored, and the way to salvation for sinners is blocked." Therefore Paul must oppose perversion rather than please men. *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-not-to-believe-an-angel)*

---

### vv. 11–12: *"For I certify to you, brothers, that the gospel I preached was not devised by man. I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it; rather, I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ."*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul now shifts from defending his apostleship to defending the divine origin of his gospel. The two stand or fall together. "Not according to man" means the gospel neither originated in human thinking nor was transmitted to Paul through human teaching. He received it "by revelation from Jesus Christ" — referring to his encounter on the Damascus Road (Acts 9) and the subsequent three days of blindness, during which Christ directly revealed the gospel to him. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill adds that Paul could not have received the gospel from the Jewish leaders who encouraged his persecution, nor from the apostles (since he avoided Jerusalem). It was a direct, divine revelation. *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** "Paul's apostleship is not from man, and his gospel is not from man. On the contrary, the risen Christ… had commissioned Paul as an apostle and had revealed to him the gospel." Paul's gospel "didn't come out of Paul's head; it came out of God's heart." *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/this-is-not-mans-gospel)*

---

### vv. 13–14: *"For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it. I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers."*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul offers his pre-conversion life as proof that his gospel did not come from human sources. He was so deeply embedded in Judaism — exceeding his peers in zeal for the "traditions of the fathers" (the oral law and Pharisaic interpretations) — that nothing in his background could have produced the gospel of grace. He was a persecutor, not a seeker. His radical 180-degree turn is only explicable by divine intervention. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill: "He could not have the Gospel, as not from nature and education, so not from the chief priests, Scribes, and elders, who encouraged him to persecute." *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

---

### vv. 15–16: *"But when God, who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by His grace, was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles, I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood,"*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul's conversion was no accident — God "set me apart from my mother's womb" (echoing Jeremiah 1:5), indicating divine election and predestination. "Called me by His grace" — the effectual call was entirely of grace. The phrase "reveal His Son in me" (not merely "to me") suggests an inward, transformative revelation, not just external vision. The purpose was apostolic: "that I might preach Him among the Gentiles." Paul's response was immediate and independent — he "did not rush to consult with flesh and blood" (any human advisor). *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill explicitly links v. 15 to "the sovereign will of God in divine predestination, and the moving cause of it, the free grace of God." *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon applied "consult not with flesh and blood" to believers today regarding baptism and church membership: "Nothing is more plainly taught in the New Testament than that it is the duty of every believer in Christ to be baptized… do your Master's will, and consult not with flesh and blood." *(Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_galatians)*

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Guzik emphasizes the supernatural directness — no human intermediary, no waiting for Jerusalem's approval. The charismatic stream often highlights this as a paradigm for direct divine calling. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

---

### v. 17: *"nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who came before me, but I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus."*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul underscores his independence from the Jerusalem apostles. After his conversion, instead of seeking their instruction or validation, he went to "Arabia" — likely the Nabatean kingdom south of Damascus. Many commentators believe Paul spent this time in solitude, receiving further revelation and being taught by the Lord, paralleling Moses' time in Midian or Elijah's time at Horeb. He then returned to Damascus, where he began preaching (Acts 9:20–22). *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill says Paul "went into Arabia preaching the Gospel." *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

---

### vv. 18–20: *"Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother. I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie."*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul waited three years before even visiting Jerusalem. The Greek verb translated "to confer" (*historeō*) means "to visit for the purpose of becoming acquainted with" — it is not the word for receiving instruction. His visit was brief (15 days) and he saw only Peter (Cephas) and James. This timeline demolishes the charge that Paul got his gospel secondhand from the Jerusalem apostles. The solemn oath "before God… no lie" shows how seriously Paul took these charges against his apostolic integrity. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill: "It was three years after his conversion, that he went to Jerusalem to visit Peter; and his stay with him was very short, no longer than fifteen days; and he was the only apostle he saw there, excepting James, the brother of Christ." *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

**Catholic reading:** Not retrieved due to search limits. Catholic commentators sometimes note James's prominence here ("the Lord's brother") as relevant to discussions of Mary's perpetual virginity and James's role as first bishop of Jerusalem.

---

### vv. 21–24: *"Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. They only heard the account: 'The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.' And they glorified God because of me."*

**Traditional reading:**

Paul continued to stay away from Judea, working in Syria and Cilicia (his home region, around Tarsus). The Judean churches didn't even know him by face — further proof he received nothing from them. All they knew was the report of his conversion, which caused them to glorify God, not Paul. The point: the Judean churches recognized Paul's gospel as genuine and glorified God for it — a powerful rebuttal to the Judaizers. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/)*

Gill: "All they knew of him was by hearsay only… wherefore it was a clear case he had not received the Gospel from them. Besides, as they had heard that he preached the Gospel of Christ, they glorified God for it, who had revealed it to him." *(Gill — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/galatians/1.htm)*

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** "If Paul had been an understudy of the apostles in Jerusalem, these are precisely the churches where he would have worked. But they don't even know him. Therefore, the whole attempt of the Judaizers to discredit Paul's independent apostleship is a failure." *(Desiring God — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/this-is-not-mans-gospel)*

## Denominational Distinctives

### Where Protestant traditions differ on Galatians 1

The core message of Galatians 1 — Paul's apostolic authority, the divine origin of the gospel, and the exclusivity of the gospel of grace — is substantially agreed upon across Protestant traditions. The chapter is a defense of the gospel itself against legalism, and all major Protestant groups (Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Lutheran, Anglican) read it this way. Differences emerge more in Galatians 2–5 (justification, law/gospel, perseverance).

What I could gather on distinctives:

- **Lutheran:** Martin Luther famously called Galatians "my Catherine von Bora" — he was "married to it." For Luther, Galatians 1 was the banner chapter for *sola gratia* and the rejection of any human addition to the gospel. Luther's reading shaped the Reformation's understanding of Paul's apostolic authority and the curse on false gospels. *(Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-1/ ; Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-1-commentary)*. Further Lutheran-specific commentary from LCMS.org or 1517.org was not reached due to search limits.

- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon applied v. 16 ("consult not with flesh and blood") to the believer's duty to be baptized and join the church without hesitating over human opinions — a distinctively Baptist application. *(Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_galatians)*. Fuller Baptist resources from gty.org or desiringgod.org were partially retrieved.

- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** Not retrieved due to search limits.

- **Catholic and Orthodox:** Not retrieved due to search limits.

- **Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes):** Not retrieved due to search limits.

- **Hyper-grace / Prosperity / Word of Faith readings:** Not retrieved from the approved sites due to search limits. These movements are occasionally criticized by the sources retrieved (e.g., Enduring Word and Precept Austin warn against any "different gospel" that adds works or denies the sufficiency of grace), but no page specifically engaging hyper-grace interpretations of Galatians 1 was found.
